entry.title: Sally Rooney Stands By Her Principles
entry.summary: Sally Rooney, one of the most popular novelists alive, says she will no longer sell her books in the U.K. In 2025, the British government proscribed Palestine Action as a terrorist organization, and in August of that year, Rooney published an op-ed in The Irish Times titled, "I support Palestine Action. If this makes me a ‘supporter of terror’ under UK law, so be it." Now, because the laws have not changed, Rooney and her publisher Faber & Faber announced this week that they will no longer be publishing her work in the U.K. Rooney's novels have sold more than 2 million copies in the U.K. alone, a monumental number for any modern novelist. Her books Normal People and Conversations with Friends have been adapted for television. In her op-ed last year, Rooney stated that she intended to give the royalties from her books sold in the U.K., as well as her residuals from the television adaptions of her novels, to Palestine Action, a direct action network known for disrupting weapon manufacturers that sell arms to Israel. Under U.K. anti-terrorism laws, Rooney's publisher can no longer give her the royalties for her novels, knowing that she will donate them to Palestine Action, without putting them both at risk. Technically, Rooney's books could still be sold in the U.K., but she would not be paid for their sales. Her publisher did not want to withhold the earnings from her. "As such, and in full agreement with Sally, we have taken the decision that we can no longer supply her works in the UK in any format," Faber & Faber said in a statement.

entry.title: Spain Reminds The USWNT Where They Stand
entry.summary: CHESTER, Penn. — For decades, the U.S. Women's National Team stood at the top of the mountain, where the air is thinnest. They defended their position with ferocity. They didn't win every major tournament, but they won most of them, and were contenders in all. Their identity on the pitch, more than anything, was being the best. That changed with the 2023 World Cup, when the two-time defending champions flamed out in the round of 16 after barely surviving the group stage. Spain went on to win the tournament, deservedly so. That result, combined with Spaniard-heavy Barcelona's simultaneous surge on the European stage, made it clear that La Roja had pushed the USWNT off the side of the mountain and taken their place at the summit. The USWNT might have won the 2024 Olympics, but anyone with eyes that see will tell you that Spain remains the better team. The USWNT are under no illusions about this. "All of these things that we're teaching are for this opponent," head coach Emma Hayes told her players Saturday after losing to Spain, 2-0, in the first of two friendlies. "And the reason I say that is because that's our barometer of success."

entry.title: Warhammer 40K Is Cool
entry.summary: In the grim darkness of the far future, 40,000 years from now, an immortal corpse-Emperor sits atop his Golden Throne on Earth, watching over the trillions upon trillions of human beings scattered across the galaxy. For ten thousand years, the Emperor hasn’t spoken or moved from that Golden Throne, and those masses of humans are ruled by the Imperium of Man in the Emperor’s name. Their often short existences are spent within the Imperium’s authoritarian systems that value ignorance over knowledge and stasis over change. Human life is cheap, and the Imperium spends it freely on never-ending wars with a variety of aliens and the forces of Chaos, which inhabit an alternate dimension known as the Warp. Earth—Terra—is a hellscape, a city-planet packed with so many people that an accurate count is impossible, its oceans long since boiled away and its original surface buried beneath millennia of haphazard construction. The Imperium is a creaking, ramshackle realm where cruelty, hierarchy, and suppression are facts of life. Its greatest warriors, the Space Marines, are genetically altered monstrosities, created through processes that kill more than they successfully manufacture. Technology is controlled by closed-minded zealots who fear nothing more than innovation. Of course, the Imperium has an Inquisition, which roots out heresy of all kinds, and an official church (the Ecclesiarchy) dedicated to unquestioning worship of the Emperor. The aliens—xenos, in the parlance of the universe—are no better. The Orks live only for fighting; the elf-like Aeldari care little for lesser beings; their dark elf Drukhari cousins subsist on torture and pain; the Necrons are living-metal horrors who traded mortal life for soulless immortality tens of millions of years ago; the insectoid Tyranids, controlled by a hivemind, exist solely to consume every bit of biomass in their path; and even the T’au, the newest addition to the galaxy, who value the Greater Good above all, aren’t to be trusted.

entry.title: Punch Bowl Now More Turd Than Punch
entry.summary: How quickly can the owner of a reigning championship team spend down a sudden windfall of goodwill? James Dolan has spent the NBA offseason exploring that hypothetical, and he appears to be a gifted speedrunner. The owner of the New York Knicks began his work before the job was even done this past June, inviting Donald Trump to Game 3 of the NBA Finals. That wound up being the team's only loss in an otherwise torrid 15-game playoff stretch. Then, at the team's victory parade, mere days after he'd funded the first title in 53 years for a team beloved by America's biggest city, Dolan took the mic and glowered. To cap off an event that united an estimated 2 million fans in communal joy, the team owner used his time in the pulpit to (predictably) take a shot at Mayor Zohran Mamdani and (inexplicably) question the Knicks fandom of parade attendees. "I don't need your vote," he told the fans, for some reason. For all the justified criticisms of Dolan over the years, he has typically been willing to spend his money on the team. A fan could have reasonably expected that an owner who has already spent big on some catastrophic Knicks rosters would happily spend big to return a lucrative, championship-winning roster, even under the current collective bargaining agreement, which punishes high spenders. But this was not the case. Just four days after the Knicks lifted the trophy, Dolan told WFAN that he would not spend into the second apron to keep the team intact. "We're willing to stretch, but there's certain things in the NBA that you'd have to be suicidal to do," he said. "One of them is the second apron."

entry.title: Irreal: Org-ibullets
entry.summary:
a simple package that trades Org mode’s heading stars for UTF-8 bullets. If you’re like me, your first thought is, “Doesn’t that already exist?” Sort of. What already exists is the no longer maintained org-bullets. Cherti’s package is called org-ibullets (note the i).
Cherti explains the differences from org-bullets in his announcement. The TL;DR is that he’s optimized org-ibullets by eliminating redundant computations, eliminated spurious syntax warnings that org-bullets could produce, and made some improvements at the source level.
As I said, the package is simple. It can be used right out of the box but you can customize the list of bullets and their face if you desire. This seems like a very nice package if you’d like to make your Org buffers look a little nicer.

There’s no shortage of Clojure REPLs, so it’s fair to ask. The smarts live on the server. When cider-nrepl is there neorepl uses it, the same way CIDER does, and when it isn’t it falls back to nREPL’s built-in ops, and then to evaluating a bit of code. entry.title: Irreal: Still More On Entering Ranges
entry.summary:
quick post on Sacha’s solution to a problem posed by David Pape. I thought it was a nice solution but then 0-_-0_ pointed out that abo-abo had already solved this problem with his tiny library. So I wrote about that and prepared to move on.
I was not allowed to. Frequent commenter Phil remarked in my original post that he would use a keyboard macro. He suggested that that would make sense for those of us who who seldom need to enter a sequence of ranges like Pape. In Pape’s case this was something that he needed to do a lot so a solution like Sacha’s or abo-abo’s make sense. I agree with Phil. A keyboard macro is exactly how I would solve this problem given that I seldom have it.
This seems pretty obvious and might not be worth writing about except that Phil’s solution showed me something that I didn’t know: You can set the initial value of the counter with a Ctrl+u n where n is the desired initial value. That’s a lot easier than using Ctrl+x Ctrl+k Ctrl+c to do the job.
As a final note, I think that Phil had a typo in his macro. As far as I can tell it should be
C-u 47 <f3> # <f3> , SPC <f4> <f4> <f4> <f4> <f4> <f4> <f4> <f4>
At least that’s what works for me.
It turns out that I regularly use a macro with a counter so I’m really happy to learn that the counter can be set so easily.
Update [2026-10-10 Sat 12:12]: Fixed link.

entry.title: James Dyer: Org Speed Keys: Making t Land After the TODO Keyword
entry.summary:
org-use-speed-commands all the time when navigating and performing actions on org headlines, but I think I have found a friction point, something that just feels a little off.
When the point is on * and then you press the key t, it calls org-todo via org-self-insert-command. Fast, but the feel is off, the point stays on the stars, so I have to move right before I can type the headline.
The reason is in org-todo itself. It has a cursor fixup that parks point just after the keyword, but only when point is not at beginning of line. Speed keys by definition run at beginning of line (org-speed-command-activate requires (bolp)), so the fixup never fires for exactly the keys that would benefit most.
There is no custom option for it, so I added a small :after advice:
(defun my/org-todo-stop-after-keyword (&rest _) "Move point to just after TODO keyword when `org-todo' leaves it at BOL. Speed command `t' (via `org-self-insert-command') runs with point at beginning of headline, where `org-todo' skips its cursor fixup." (when (and (bolp) (org-at-heading-p)) (when (looking-at org-todo-line-regexp) (goto-char (or (match-end 2) (match-end 1))) (when (looking-at " ") (forward-char 1))))) (advice-add 'org-todo :after #'my/org-todo-stop-after-keyword)
* Test with point on * plus t becomes * TODO Test with point on Test, ready to type. Same for cycling * TODO to * DONE.
Small change, but speed keys finally feel like they finish the job instead of leaving me parked on the margin!

entry.title: Curtis McHale: Emacs Carnival - Will we change how we interact with Emacs?
entry.summary: Will voice kill the keyboard. No. Will the way we interact with Emacs, and computers in general, change drastically? No. Star Trek has a mythical AI/computer that responds to voice commands and interacts with you to clarify or note other work that may pertain to what you wanted. Evidently the interface is so ubiquitous that Scotty talks to a mouse noting it's "quaint" to need to push it and type on a keyboard to interact with a computer. But if we watch the bridge of any Star Trek show people aren't talking the whole time. They're tapping screens to get the computer to do things for them. Theoretically the captain could tell the ship where he wants to go and let the computer do it, but he issues a command and then someone types in the needed commands to the ship so it goes in the expected direction. I work at home in a solo office space. I could talk to my computer and it would disturb no one, except me. I'd be unable to listen to music on my stereo at the same time just in case the computer couldn't understand my words versus the song. I don't think keyboards are going anywhere any time soon. They provide an unambiguous interface to your computer that doesn't disturb others. I think that those loving Emacs interactions like they use it will continue to do so as they do now because it's the most efficient way to control the Emacs interface.

entry.title: I tried to move my notes out of Emacs. I failed. Again.
entry.summary: Every so often I suffer from what I call "Emacs Fatigue". It's closely related to "Text File Fatigue". Using Emacs tends to pull one toward using it for everything, which is what I'd done. Then, I simply grow tired of staring at the same thing every day. When this happens, I "decide" to uproot my life and move my notes into something else. This time, that something else was Bear. Bear is great. It's solid, beautiful, and refreshingly simple. It syncs flawlessly (for free[1]) and runs on macOS and iOS. It's also inexpensive. It uses an SQLite database, which doesn't bother me. Databases are great at this stuff. All the "But but what if the database...?!" talk is mostly hearsay anyway. The thing that made me twitchy was that it felt like my notes were "in there". It's not the database. It's the fact that everything is in an app, and that app makes me need to use that app. This is how I'd started to feel about Emacs, but mostly due to Org mode. Bear is macOS and iOS only, which should be fine for someone like me who has "decided" to live on macOS. And yet, Linux continues to emit a low-grade hum in the back of my head that I can't ignore. If I don't want my notes in Org mode files, but I'm still drawn toward Emacs, what should I do? Denote! That's where they'd all started in the first place, but as .org not .md. I'd nearly forgotten that Denote handles Markdown files natively. One Emacs configuration change and I was back where I belong. And since Bear notes are already Markdown, all it took was an export and a (Claude Code-assisted) conversion script for file names, links, and attachments. So yes, I've done that thing where I quit using Emacs only to come crawling back later. I know better, but knowing better doesn't stop me. Maybe I'll work on a sync/bridge between Denote and Bear. That would be neat. It was pointed out that Bear isn't free, so syncing isn't free. True, but I guess meant that it's not a paid extra. ↩︎ ✍️ Reply by email

entry.title: Irreal: Inserting Number Ranges As A List
entry.summary:
very nice solution to a problem posed by David Pape: how can we enter a range of numbers as list of distinct numbers in Emacs? Pape’s specific problem was entering the numbers of error reports that a Git commit closes. Rather than entering something like
closes: 47, 48, 49, 50, 51, 70
he’d like to enter something like
closes: 47-51 70
and call an Emacs function to have it expanded into the first example.
Chua has a very nice solution that covers that case as well things like
47-51, 70
or even
5-15/2
to expand into the sequence
5, 7, 9, 11, 13, 15
Most of the heavy lifting is done by the number-sequence function. The rest of the work is parsing the input string into either a single number or a range of numbers that number-sequence can work on.
Chua’s solution strikes me as an example of Emacs at its best. The problem it solves is not earth shattering. It’s simply a bit of friction in a user’s everyday workflow but Emacs easily provides a solution that makes the friction disappear. Take a look at her code. It not only shows an ingenious solution to the problem but also demonstrates the power of Emacs and Elisp to make the application of that genius simple.

entry.title: Irreal: The Power Of Plain Text
entry.summary:
extolling the power of plain text. It’s a notion that’s familiar to all us Emacs users and even more so to Org users. We Org users (or more generally Markdown and other markup users) can write plain text and have it formatted for output in a variety of ways. The point is, the text stays text and is readable even without the formatting.
As nickb says, text written today will still be readable 50 years from now. Sure, UTF-8 and the other Unicode formats can and do add new characters from time to time but text written today will have the same meaning even if new characters are added.
The most important aspect is that you’ll own your data no matter what programs come and go. Emacs isn’t going anywhere but even if it did, it wouldn’t matter. Text will still be readable and something like Org or Markdown will still make intended formatting obvious even if Org and Markdown no longer exist.
Nickb acknowledges that text is not the right answer for everything. You wouldn’t, for example, want to represent a photograph in plain text and there are lots of other examples. Still, for many applications, plain text is not only sufficient but probably the better solution.

entry.title: Sacha Chua: Emacs Lisp: Parse page ranges, insert issue references
entry.summary:
David Pape asked:
I just typed
>Closes: #47, #48, #49, #50, #51, #52, #53, #54
into a commit description, all by hand.
Is there a way in Emacs to expand some kind of range description to make this easier? 😅
I want to expand strings like "5-10, 15-18, 3" into numbers.
Hmm, could be useful. It reminds me of how page ranges work, which will be handy if I want to tinker with PDFs. Let's see if something like this works:
(defun sacha-parse-page-range (s) "Parse a page range string and return a list of numbers. Ex: 1-5 2-4, 6-10 1 4 7-9 3-11/2 - this one specifies an increment" (seq-mapcat (lambda (part) (let ((nums (mapcar 'string-to-number (split-string part " *[-/] *")))) (if (= (length nums) 1) nums (number-sequence (elt nums 0) (elt nums 1) (elt nums 2))))) (split-string s "[, \t\n\r]+")))
(ert-deftest sacha-parse-page-range () (should (equal (sacha-parse-page-range "5-10") '(5 6 7 8 9 10))) (should (equal (sacha-parse-page-range "1-5, 8") '(1 2 3 4 5 8))) (should (equal (sacha-parse-page-range "1 4 7-9") '(1 4 7 8 9))) (should (equal (sacha-parse-page-range "3-11/2") '(3 5 7 9 11))))
(defun sacha-issue-range (range) "Expand RANGE to a list of issues and insert them." (interactive "MRange (ex: 1-5, 7): ") (let ((s (mapconcat (lambda (n) (format "#%d" n)) (sacha-parse-page-range range) ", "))) (when (called-interactively-p 'any) (insert s)) s))
How to use abo-abo/tiny to expand "m47, 54|#%d" Inserting Number Ranges As A List | Irreal More On Number Ranges | Irreal Still More On Entering Ranges | Irreal This is part of my EmacsConfiguration. View Org source for this post You can e-mail me at sacha@sachachua.com.

entry.title: Charles Choi: Announcing triode.el
entry.summary:
A long-standing passion of mine is listening to and collecting music. I’m always on the lookout for new music and where I discover it is primarily from internet radio stations. That said, listening to music in such a way is largely a passive activity, where your main focus is somewhere else. The better music players that acknowledge this difference in focus provide mechanisms for remote-controlling them from other apps. So it is with the Triode app for macOS, which leverages Cocoa frameworks (App Intents in particular) to support remote control. triode.el is an Emacs Lisp library which provides a simple remote control interface to the Triode app. Basic support for selecting a radio station, play/stop, and muting are provided. Not every feature in the Triode app is accessible to triode.el though; this is controlled by the App Intents actually implemented by its developer, The Iconfactory.
Interested readers can learn more about triode.el in its user guide. triode.el is now available on MELPA. This release joins my other packages that support remote control of music apps on macOS from Emacs: now-playing.el - Interface for the Music app. shazam.el - Interface for Shazam music recognition. All the above efforts have been an exploration of malleable computing using Emacs as the main orchestration tool. I plan on posting a more technical deep dive reflecting this work in the not too distant future. That said, if you’re a macOS user who uses Emacs and Triode, I encourage you to give triode.el a try. Also, consider this a plug for Triode app, a well-designed app that does a great job of taking advantage of the Cocoa frameworks to provide internet radio across different devices provided by Apple.

entry.title: Irreal: The Future Of Emacs
entry.summary:
What’s the future of Emacs? He asks that question in the context of assuming that Emacs will continue to exist for any timeline that matters to us. But how, he asks, will we use it?
The answer that will occur to most of us is speech mediated input á la Star Trek TNG. We’ll simply tell Emacs what we want it to do and it will do it. But think about that for a moment. Would you really want to dictate the code for your latest program to the computer? Or would you even want to dictate your documentation, story, or letter to your computer?
Sure, you could say something like, “Computer write a program to do such and such.” but then you’re not using Emacs at all. The same for asking the computer to write something for you. That—more or less—is here today but most of us don’t like the results and, again, we’re not really using Emacs in those situations.
For my part, my written thoughts are always much better organized than my spoken ones so even with capable voice input, I’d much prefer to use the keyboard. Maiorana agrees. He points back to a couple of episodes from Tales From the Darkside1 in which people use the keyboard to do magic with the computer. For him, Meta+x is the spell that enables the magic and he’s very attached to it. Like me, he doesn’t anticipate abandoning the keyboard.
What do you think? Will we still use the keyboard or will we move on to something better?
